steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - known vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks -> growing research on verifying NN safety, find fragilities before deployment
- Mitigations
  - adversarial training, verification-based augmentation
  - progress, but models still fragile to input perturbations -> limited applicability
  - inherently more robust architectures: BNNs intrinsically more resilient to adversarial attacks
  - reason: randomness in posterior distribution
- BNN verification
  - still need to verify safety/correctness incl. robustness before deployment
  - deterministic NNs: safety a decision problem; BNNs: probabilistic
  - probabilistic robustness: given BNN, input region, safe set -> probability input neighbourhood mapped to safe set
  - also called probabilistic safety problem
  - exact computation intractable -> approximation approaches
- Challenge + contributions
  - approximate tightly and efficiently; existing methods loose or expensive (shown in Sections 3, 4)
  - Pure Iterative Expansion (PIE), Gradient-guided Iterative Expansion (GIE): sound lower bounds, provably tighter than SoA sampling-based
  - evaluation on MNIST, CIFAR10: tighter approximations
  - code in supplementary material
  - outline: Subsection 1 related work; Section 2 definitions; Section 3 approach (PIE/GIE in 3.2, tightness proof in 3.3); Section 4 evaluation
## Related Work
- MILP + Bound Propagation (BP) for standard NNs
  - MILP: encode verification as MILP, MILP solvers; assumes piecewise-linear activations
  - propagation: relaxed network, propagate bounds through layers
  - SoA combines both: bound propagation + adaptive splitting -> fewer binary variables, faster
- Robustness: same output in small neighbourhood of input
  - upper bounds on BNN robustness
  - probability that a nearby input changes the prediction; approximation + statistical guarantees
  - gradient-based attack vulnerability of BNNs from data on lower-dimensional submanifold
  - sampling-based: sample orthotopes from posterior, IBP + LBP to check safety, repeat -> certificate + lower bound
  - Lagrangian duality with functional multipliers: exact in optimum, impractical; lower bounds for specific multiplier classes
  - Dynamic Programming + bound propagation + convex relaxations: lower/upper bounds on predictions
  - extension of sampling-based algorithm: upper bounds too; handles unbounded-support posteriors
  - MILP for infinite time-horizon safety, small networks only
  - credal BNNs via constraint relaxation over probabilistic circuits

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, Neural Networks (NNs) have been proposed for performing safety-critical functions in applications like automated driving, medical image processing and others. Assurance and certification are paramount if machine learning methods are going to be adopted in these areas.

NNs are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, and following this a fast growing body of research has focused on methods to verify the safety of NNs so that fragilities can be identified before deployment.

Several methods have been proposed to mitigate the vulnerabilities of NNs to adversarial attacks, including adversarial training and verification-based augmentation. A lot of progress has been made in these areas, but present models are still fragile to various input perturbations, and this limits their potential applicability in key areas.

To try to overcome this problem, architectures that are more robust inherently have been proposed. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have arguably become a key class of models that are intrinsically more resilient to adversarial attacks. The reason is that BNNs naturally incorporate the randomness that is present in the posterior distribution.

BNNs have been shown to give a degree of natural robustness, but it is still crucial to verify their safety and correctness with respect to specifications of interest, including robustness, before they are deployed. While safety is formulated as a standard decision problem for deterministic NNs, for BNNs safety is a probabilistic concept. Specifically, given a BNN, an input region and a safe set, the probabilistic robustness problem is about determining the probability that the BNN maps the input neighbourhood to a safe set.

The probabilistic robustness problem for BNNs is sometimes also called the probabilistic safety problem. Computing probabilistic robustness for BNNs exactly is computationally intractable, so several approaches have been proposed to approximate it.

- Challenge + contributions
  - approximate tightly + efficiently; existing methods loose or expensive (Sections 3, 4)
  - PIE + GIE: sound lower bounds, provably tighter than SoA sampling-based
  - MNIST, CIFAR10 evaluation: tighter approximations; code in supplementary material
  - outline: Subsection 1 related work; Section 2 definitions; Section 3 approach (PIE/GIE in 3.2, tightness in 3.3); Section 4 evaluation
## Related Work
- MILP vs. bound propagation for standard NNs; SoA combines them (bound propagation + adaptive splitting, fewer binary variables)
- Robustness specification; upper bounds for BNN robustness; probability of a prediction-changing nearby input + statistical guarantees
- BNN vulnerability to gradient attacks: data on lower-dimensional submanifold
- sampling-based orthotopes + IBP/LBP -> certificate + lower bound
- Lagrangian duality with functional multipliers: exact but impractical; lower bounds for some multiplier classes
- Dynamic Programming + bound propagation + convex relaxations; extension of sampling approach to upper bounds and unbounded-support posteriors
- MILP for infinite time-horizon safety (small networks only); credal BNNs via probabilistic circuits

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, Neural Networks (NNs) have been proposed for performing safety-critical functions in applications like automated driving, medical image processing and others. Assurance and certification are paramount if machine learning methods are going to be adopted in these areas.

NNs are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks, and following this a fast growing body of research has focused on methods to verify the safety of NNs so that fragilities can be identified before deployment.

Several methods have been proposed to mitigate the vulnerabilities of NNs to adversarial attacks, including adversarial training and verification-based augmentation. A lot of progress has been made in these areas, but present models are still fragile to various input perturbations, and this limits their potential applicability in key areas.

To try to overcome this problem, architectures that are more robust inherently have been proposed. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have arguably become a key class of models that are intrinsically more resilient to adversarial attacks. The reason is that BNNs naturally incorporate the randomness that is present in the posterior distribution.

BNNs have been shown to give a degree of natural robustness, but it is still crucial to verify their safety and correctness with respect to specifications of interest, including robustness, before they are deployed. While safety is formulated as a standard decision problem for deterministic NNs, for BNNs safety is a probabilistic concept. Specifically, given a BNN, an input region and a safe set, the probabilistic robustness problem is about determining the probability that the BNN maps the input neighbourhood to a safe set.

The probabilistic robustness problem for BNNs is sometimes also called the probabilistic safety problem. Computing probabilistic robustness for BNNs exactly is computationally intractable, so several approaches have been proposed to approximate it.

A key challenge here is to approximate the probabilistic robustness of BNNs tightly and efficiently. As we show in Sections 3 and 4, existing methods are either loose or computationally expensive. So it is still of great interest to explore new approaches that can derive tighter approximations to probabilistic robustness and still be computationally effective. To this end, our contributions in this paper are as follows.

- We introduce two new algorithms, Pure Iterative Expansion (PIE) and Gradient-guided Iterative Expansion (GIE). We show that they give sound lower bounds on the probabilistic robustness of BNNs, and these bounds are provably tighter than SoA sampling-based approaches.

- We evaluate our algorithms empirically on MNIST and CIFAR10 benchmarks against the SoA and show that our approach gives tighter approximations of the probabilistic robustness.

- We provide our code in the supplementary material for reproducibility.

The rest of the paper is organised like this. Subsection 1 reviews the related literature on NN and BNN verification. Section 2 formally defines BNNs, the probabilistic robustness problem for BNNs, and other related terminology that we use throughout the paper. Section 3 discusses the details of our approach, and in Subsection 3.2 it introduces the PIE and GIE algorithms for exploring the set of safe weights and computing lower bounds for the probabilistic robustness of BNNs. In Subsection 3.3 we also show formally that our approach outperforms the SoA sampling-based method by producing provably tighter bounds. Section 4 evaluates the performance of our approach against SoA on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets.

## Related Work

Two common techniques used for verifying standard NNs are Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) and Bound Propagation (BP). In MILP-based approaches, the NN verification problem is encoded as an MILP problem, and this can be solved with MILP solvers. These approaches commonly assume that activations are piecewise-linear.

Propagation-based approaches are different from MILP-based ones because they consider a relaxed network and propagate bounds on the output of each node through the layers of the network to solve the verification problem.

SoA approaches for verifying NNs combine MILP and BP to get complete and scalable verification. For example, one such method uses bound propagation together with adaptive splitting to reduce the number of binary variables in the MILP problem that results, and so it speeds up the verification process further. Robustness is an important and well-studied safety specification in NN verification, i.e., how resilient a model is in returning the same output for all values in a small neighbourhood of a given input. One example of an approach that is only devoted to checking robustness is an earlier study, where they compute upper bounds on the robustness of BNNs. Closely related to this, another work considers the problem of computing the probability of whether, for a given input to a BNN, there is another input within a bounded set around the input such that the network's prediction is different for the two points, and it gives an approach to approximate this probability and compute statistical guarantees for it.

In the same line of research, another study shows that the vulnerability of BNNs to gradient-based attacks comes from the data lying on a lower-dimensional submanifold of the ambient space.

One approach considers a set-up similar to this paper and uses a sampling-based approach to bound the probabilistic robustness of BNNs. There, orthotopes are sampled from the posterior distribution and Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) and Linear Bound Propagation (LBP) are used to determine whether a given orthotope is safe. Repeating this process gives a robustness certificate and a lower bound for the probabilistic robustness of the BNN.

Other authors consider the adversarial robustness of BNNs. They use the notion of Lagrangian duality, where standard Lagrangian multipliers are replaced with functional multipliers. With an optimal choice of functional multipliers this approach leads to exact verification, i.e., computing the probabilistic robustness exactly. But this may not be practical. The authors show however that for specific classes of multipliers one can get lower bounds for the probabilistic robustness.

A further work introduced an algorithm to verify the adversarial robustness of BNNs. It uses Dynamic Programming together with bound propagation and convex relaxations to compute lower and upper bounds on BNN predictions for a given input set. A follow-up builds on the algorithm first presented in the sampling-based work above to give upper bounds on the probabilistic robustness of BNNs in addition to lower bounds. They also extend the algorithmic formulation in that work to handle the specification proposed in the duality-based work on posterior distributions with unbounded support.

Another approach uses MILP to get robustness guarantees for infinite time-horizon safety and robustness of BNNs. But it can only be used for small networks. Finally, one work gets robustness guarantees for credal BNNs via constraint relaxation over probabilistic circuits.

steps.text:
In recent years, Neural Networks (NNs) have been proposed to perform safety-critical functions in applications such as automated driving, medical image processing and beyond [1,2,3,4]. For machine learning methods to be adopted in these areas, assurance and certification are paramount.

Following the known vulnerabilities of NNs to adversarial attacks [5,6,7,8,9], a rapidly growing body of research has focused on methods for verifying the safety of NNs [10,11,12,13,14,15] in order to identify fragilities before deployment.

To mitigate the vulnerabilities of NNs to adversarial attacks, several methods have been proposed, including adversarial training [13,16,17,18] and verification-based augmentation [19]. While considerable progress has been made in these areas, present models remain fragile to various input perturbations, which limits their potential applicability in key areas.

In an attempt to overcome this problem, inherently more robust architectures have been proposed. Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) have arguably emerged as a key class of models that are intrinsically more resilient to adversarial attacks [20,21]. This is because BNNs naturally incorporate the randomness present in the posterior distribution [22].

Although BNNs have been shown to provide a degree of natural robustness, it is crucial to verify their safety and correctness with respect to specifications of interest, including robustness, before deployment. Note that while safety is formulated as a standard decision problem in deterministic NNs, for BNNs safety is a probabilistic concept. Specifically, given a BNN, an input region and a safe set, the probabilistic robustness problem concerns determining the probability that the input neighbourhood is mapped to the safe set by the BNN [23,24,25].

The probabilistic robustness problem for BNNs is also sometimes referred to as the probabilistic safety problem [24]. Since exactly computing probabilistic robustness for BNNs is computationally intractable, several approaches for approximating it have been proposed [25,26,27].

A key challenge in this area is to approximate the probabilistic robustness of BNNs tightly and efficiently. As we demonstrate in Sections 3 and 4, existing methods are either loose or computationally expensive. It therefore remains of great interest to explore new approaches that derive tighter approximations to probabilistic robustness while remaining computationally effective. To this end, our contributions in this paper can be summarised as follows.

- • We introduce two new algorithms, Pure Iterative Expansion (PIE) and Gradient-guided Iterative Expansion (GIE). We show that they produce sound lower bounds on the probabilistic robustness of BNNs which are provably tighter than SoA sampling-based approaches.

- • We empirically evaluate our algorithms against the SoA on MNIST and CIFAR10 benchmarks and show that our approach produces tighter approximations of the probabilistic robustness.

- • For reproducibility, our code is provided in the supplementary material.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In Subsection 1, we review the related literature on NN and BNN verification. In Section 2, we formally define BNNs, the probabilistic robustness problem for BNNs, and other related terminology used throughout the paper. We discuss the details of our approach in Section 3, introducing the PIE and GIE algorithms for exploring the set of safe weights and computing lower bounds for the probabilistic robustness of BNNs in Subsection 3.2. In Subsection 3.3 we also formally show that our approach outperforms the SoA sampling-based method by producing provably tighter bounds. We evaluate the performance of our approach against SoA on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets in Section 4.

## Related Work

Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) and Bound Propagation (BP) are two common techniques for the verification of standard NNs. In MILP-based approaches, the verification problem for NNs is encoded as an MILP problem [11,28,29], which can then be solved using MILP solvers. A common assumption in MILP-based approaches is that activations are piecewise-linear.

Propagation-based approaches differ from MILP-based approaches in that they consider a relaxed network and propagate bounds on the output of each node through the layers of the network to solve the verification problem [30,31,32,33].

SoA approaches for NN verification combine MILP and BP to achieve complete and scalable verification. For instance, [34] uses bound propagation alongside adaptive splitting [35,36] to reduce the number of binary variables in the resulting MILP problem and thus further speed up verification. An important and well-studied safety specification in NN verification is robustness, i.e., the resilience of a model in returning the same output for all values in a small neighbourhood of a given input. An example of an approach devoted only to checking robustness is [24], where they compute upper bounds on the robustness of BNNs. Closely related to this, [23] considers the problem of computing the probability of whether, for a given input to a BNN, there exists another input within a bounded set around it such that the prediction of the network differs for the two points, and provides an approach to approximate this probability and compute statistical guarantees for it.

In the same line of research, [21] shows that the vulnerability of BNNs to gradient-based attacks arises from the data lying on a lower-dimensional submanifold of the ambient space.

[25] considers a set-up similar to this paper, using a sampling-based approach to bound the probabilistic robustness of BNNs. In this approach, they sample orthotopes from the posterior distribution and use Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) and Linear Bound Propagation (LBP) to determine whether a given orthotope is safe. By repeating this process, they obtain a robustness certificate and a lower bound for the probabilistic robustness of the BNN.

[26] consider the adversarial robustness of BNNs. They use the notion of Lagrangian duality, replacing standard Lagrangian multipliers with functional multipliers. For an optimal choice of functional multipliers, this approach leads to exact verification, i.e., the exact computation of probabilistic robustness, but this may not be practical. The authors show, however, that for specific classes of multipliers one can obtain lower bounds for the probabilistic robustness.

[37] introduced an algorithm for verifying the adversarial robustness of BNNs. They use Dynamic Programming alongside bound propagation and convex relaxations to compute lower and upper bounds on BNN predictions for a given input set. [38] build on the algorithm first presented in [25] to provide upper bounds on the probabilistic robustness of BNNs in addition to lower bounds. Moreover, they extend the algorithmic formulation in [25] to handle the specification proposed in [26] on posterior distributions with unbounded support.

[27] uses MILP to obtain robustness guarantees for infinite time-horizon safety and robustness of BNNs, but this approach can only be used for small networks. [39] obtains robustness guarantees for credal BNNs via constraint relaxation over probabilistic circuits.
